items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — the call opened 'This is Chris with Einstein Moving Company. How can I help you?' and went straight into 'let me check this out real quick' with no roadmap, no timeframe, and no confirmation the customer was ready to run through details.
Never asked 'how are you today?' The customer asked Chris — 'Hey Chris, how are you?' — and Chris answered 'Doing good.' without returning the question.

Customer's name was never obtained or spoken. Chris worked the whole call off a cloned file and closed with 'what was the pleasure getting to work with you' rather than using the name, which was available on the record.

Origin and destination were never verbally confirmed. The customer said 'It's actually going from the same address to the same address,' then his answer to the stops question came through as 'So, she's Illinois to will I?' and Chris responded 'Okay, let me clone this real quick' — he cloned a three-stop job without reading a single address back for confirmation.
No stairs or floors question at either end, and no access questions (parking, elevator, gate) — on a job he then committed to a firm $525 budget.
No walk-distance question, despite the customer describing 'an outdoor plastic storage cabinet... what you put in a car port' — a carport item implies a curb-to-truck carry that was never sized.

Packing needs never asked, and the box count was left genuinely open. The customer said 'TBD, cause we may move a lot of it ourselves... I just don't really know what's in there until I get a chance to go' — Chris pinned it to '5:00 to ten' but never asked whether they wanted packing help or offered to adjust if the number grew.
No moving-stressor question — 'Is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' was never asked.

No 'pricing is super simple' framing, and no what's-included list — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools were never mentioned. The rate landed bare as 'it's a 210 hourly rate' in the last thirty seconds of the call.
Disassembly/reassembly never mentioned as included, even though the inventory is 'One bed queen' plus 'one very small Chester drawers' — a bed frame is the textbook assembly item.
No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This is a repeat customer moving a TV and a grill with no coverage conversation at all.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned. Chris got close — 'The arrival window is 145 to 345 and the crew will call you about thirty minutes out' — but stated the window without the guarantee behind it.

Clock explanation was one line out of four. 'Two and a half hour minimum' was covered twice, but there was no 'clock starts on-site when the contract opens,' no 15-minute prorated increments after the minimum, and no sense-check on any of it.
Mover and truck count never stated. The customer was quoted '$210 hourly rate' and a '$525 budget' without ever being told how many movers or trucks that buys.

Save Your Ass speech essentially absent — no 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, and no 'take a carload' tip. The customer handed him the opening outright with 'we may move a lot of it ourselves' and Chris let it pass without shaping what they should pre-move.
'No deposit required' never mentioned — a live booking closed without Einstein's headline differentiator.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections.' Chris confirmed the email address ('ihaveCharlie.Edward. S-N-Y-C. @gmail.com') but never asked the customer to verify the details once it arrived.

Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' The customer had to volunteer his own — 'you guys are just gonna send that to my email you on file, right?' — after Chris had already begun wrapping up.
Hours and how to reach us never given.

Pricing came after the booking, not before it. Chris said 'I will go and get you a move confirmation' and the customer accepted Sunday before hearing the rate — then Chris backfilled with 'Yeah, it just recap. It's a 210 hourly rate.' The customer's 'But that's fine. No worries.' is agreement, not informed agreement.
top_strength: Chris ran a genuinely efficient repeat-customer call and closed it inside 5.7 minutes. He immediately recognized the record and worked from it — 'Alright, so last time around it looks like we had three different stops what's still going to be relevant for this move?' — which is the right instinct on a returning customer and saved the customer from re-explaining a job Einstein already had on file. His availability offer was the cleanest part of the call: he gave two concrete choices with real windows rather than a vague 'let me see what we have' — 'availability tomorrow it would be in the afternoon. We could do a 2:30 to 430 start time window, if that is a little bit too late in the day, we have Sunday with a 1:45 to 345 window' — and got a commitment on the second option. He also handled two things proactively that most reps miss. First, the propane policy without being asked: he heard 'grill,' asked 'is that propane or just charcoal?', and set the expectation cleanly with a confirmation check — 'we just need you to take the propane just visits a combustible item, okay?' That is a real move-day problem prevented on the phone. Second, he went out of his way on an off-script ask, pulling the vendor list for upholstery cleaning — 'we've used hearts carpet cleaning, I would assume they do furniture as well and then also Austin specialty cleaners' — which is exactly the helpfulness the bonus section is built for. The one clear rapport moment was natural rather than scripted: when the customer paused to check with his wife, Chris said 'Yeah, yeah, take time. Yeah, yeah, yeah, I know how that goes,' and the customer came back comfortable enough to keep asking for help.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: the price came after the yes. Chris took the booking, said 'I will go and get you a move confirmation,' and only then backfilled 'Yeah, it just recap. It's a 210 hourly rate. Two and a half hour minimum. I do not foresee us going over that. So it should be a $525 budget.' Sequence that before the close, not after it, and say the whole thing: 'Pricing is super simple — it's $210 an hour for two movers and a truck, and that covers the gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands and tools, plus disassembling and reassembling that queen bed. Clock starts on-site when we open the contract, two-and-a-half hour minimum, then 15-minute increments after that — so for what you've described I'd budget $525. Does that make sense? And there's no deposit, so I can lock Sunday in right now.' That single re-ordered paragraph picks up points across pricing, clock, estimate and booking at once, and it turns an assumed yes into an informed one. Second priority: the customer told Chris exactly how to run the Save Your Ass speech and Chris walked past it. When he said 'we may move a lot of it ourselves... I just don't really know what's in there,' the line was 'Perfect — here's how to make Sunday cheaper. Anything that fits in your car, take a carload before we get there: the loose stuff in drawers, anything in that outdoor cabinet, the small odds and ends. The more you consolidate up front, the shorter the move and the lower the bill. Make sense?' On a minimum-length job that is what protects the estimate from a surprise box count. Third: use the customer's name — Chris never said it once on a call with a returning customer whose record was open in front of him — and add the two differentiators that cost nothing here: No Worries Damage Coverage (a TV and a grill are going on that truck) and the On-Time Guarantee, which slots naturally into the arrival-window line he already delivered. One operational flag: the addresses were never confirmed out loud on a cloned three-stop job, and the customer's stop answer came through garbled. Verify in EMMA that the cloned job's stop list matches what's actually happening Sunday before the crew is dispatched.
phone_presence_notes: Warm, unhurried and genuinely accommodating — 'Yeah, yeah, take time... I know how that goes' when the customer checked with his wife, a real effort on the off-script upholstery-cleaner request, and a positive customer at the close ('Thank you too. Bye-bye.') — held back from a 5 only by heavy 'Okay, okay' filler and never once using the customer's name.
audio_review_reason: The customer's side of the transcript is badly garbled at the most consequential moment — his answer about which stops still apply rendered as 'So, she's Illinois to will I?' — so it cannot be determined from text whether addresses were actually confirmed aloud before Chris cloned the job, or whether Chris asked a clarifying question that the transcript dropped.
